passages.happening:
The heading reads, “A song of ascents. Of Solomon” (verse 1). The psalm begins with two pictures of wasted work. “Unless the LORD builds the house, its builders labor in vain; unless the LORD protects the city, its watchmen stand guard in vain” (verse 1).

Then a third. “In vain you rise early and stay up late, toiling for bread to eat” (verse 2). And the reason it is in vain: “for He gives sleep to His beloved” (verse 2).

So the builder, the watchman and the worker can all labour hard and still get nowhere, if the LORD is not in it. And the one God loves can lie down and sleep.
passages.hearers:
Psalms 127 and 128 belong together. Both are about house and home, work and children. This note and the next should be read as a pair. The note on Psalm 120 explains the Songs of Ascents.

This is the only Song of Ascents headed ‘Of Solomon’. The book page explains what such headings may mean. A first hearer would catch the links. Solomon built the house of the LORD, the temple, and his own palace. The word for ‘His beloved’ in verse 2, yedid, sounds like the name God gave Solomon as a baby: Jedidiah, “because the LORD loved him” (2 Samuel 12:25). Many scholars think the heading was added by someone who noticed these links.

In that world ‘house’ meant more than a building. It meant a household: family, servants and goods. For a king it meant a line of kings. God told David, “He Himself will establish a house for you” (2 Samuel 7:11), meaning a family that would rule. So ‘building a house’ in verse 1 may also mean raising a family, which leads into verses 3 to 5.

The watchman stood on the city wall at night. Even he could not keep the city safe by himself.
passages.later:
Jesus spoke of the wise man “who built his house on the rock” (Matthew 7:24). He told of a farmer who sows seed, and then “Night and day he sleeps and wakes, and the seed sprouts and grows, though he knows not how” (Mark 4:27).

Paul wrote of his own work in the church: “I planted the seed and Apollos watered it, but God made it grow” (1 Corinthians 3:6). Jesus told his followers not to worry about food and clothes: “But seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness” (Matthew 6:33).
passages.asks:
Psalm 127 does not tell you to stop working. Builders still build, and watchmen still watch. It tells you that work without God is in vain, and that worry is not the same as work.

Are you rising early and staying up late, sure that everything depends on you? Verse 2 says that sleep is a gift. Lying down to rest can be an act of trust: God keeps the city while you sleep.

passages.t: ‘Children are indeed a heritage from the LORD’
passages.happening:
The psalm turns to children. “Children are indeed a heritage from the LORD, and the fruit of the womb is His reward” (verse 3).

Then a picture from war. “Like arrows in the hand of a warrior, so are children born in one's youth” (verse 4). “Blessed is the man whose quiver is full of them. He will not be put to shame when he confronts the enemies at the gate” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
A ‘heritage’ is an inheritance, something handed down as a gift. To call children a heritage and a reward from the LORD is to say they are given, not made. The house God builds (verse 1) includes the people in it.

Arrows in a warrior's hand were his protection. A quiver was the case that held them. In a world without pensions or police, grown children were a parent's support in old age and in trouble.

The city gate was where disputes were settled before the elders (Ruth 4:1 shows a case heard there). To face enemies ‘at the gate’ probably means facing opponents in a dispute, not in battle. A man with grown sons beside him was hard to cheat or push around.
passages.later:
Jesus welcomed children when others sent them away: “Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them!” (Matthew 19:14).

The Bible also makes room for those with no children. God promised the eunuchs, men who could have no descendants, “a name better than that of sons and daughters” in his house (Isaiah 56:5). Jesus had no children. Paul, who was single, called his state a gift: “each man has his own gift from God” (1 Corinthians 7:7). And Jesus named a family open to everyone: “whoever does the will of God is My brother and sister and mother” (Mark 3:35).
passages.hard:
A word of care. Verses 3 to 5 praise children as God's gift. They do not promise a child to everyone who prays for one, and a gift is not a wage. Many faithful people long for children and never have them, or lose them before birth. Childlessness is not a judgment from God, and it does not measure your faith. Your longing is seen. If the grief is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor.

A home without children, or a single person, is not less blessed in God's eyes. Jesus himself lived and died without wife or children. The family of God is wider than any one household, and there is a place in it for you.
passages.asks:
If you have children, Psalm 127 asks you to see them as gifts held in trust, not possessions or projects. They are arrows: made to be sent out, not kept in the quiver forever.

And whoever you are, the psalm asks who you are building with. Every believer is part of a household God is building. Who in your church or street needs you to stand beside them ‘at the gate’?
